title: Webb Telescope Spots Signs of Giant Crashes Around Young Stars
summary:
Scientists think our Moon formed after a huge crash long ago. The young Earth collided with a Mars-sized object called Theia, and some of the debris later came together to form the Moon. Now, NASA's James Webb Space Telescope is helping astronomers study young star systems where similar crashes may be happening.

A team led by Kate Su of the Space Science Institute in Boulder, Colorado, studied 21 rare "extreme debris disks." These are clouds of unusually warm dust close to young stars, in the area where rocky planets like Earth orbit in our own solar system. Five came from older data collected by NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope, and 16 were studied with Webb. The findings were published on October 1 in The Astrophysical Journal.

"This is the first time we have gathered enough systems to truly understand this subclass that we call extreme debris disks," Su said.

Scientists estimate that only about 1% of young stars show signs of this stage. Our own solar system may have gone through it, too.

The researchers studied the minerals in the dust and found two groups. About one-third of the disks are rich in silica, a material found in volcanic glass called obsidian. The team says these likely formed after extremely powerful crashes between Mars-sized worlds, strong enough to turn a lot of rock into vapor. The other two-thirds have little silica. They seem to come from gentler crashes, including glancing blows between Moon-sized objects.

The silica-rich disks were found only around stars younger than 300 million years. The silica-poor disks appear around stars of many different ages.

"We have no other way to study these planetary embryos directly because they are too small," said Agnes Kospal of Konkoly Observatory in Budapest, Hungary, a co-author of the study.
why_it_matters: Watching crashes around young stars helps scientists understand how Earth and the Moon formed. It shows that building planets can be a violent process.

background_read: The James Webb Space Telescope is a large space telescope that sees infrared light, which lets it study warm dust that is hard to see with ordinary light.
Planets form inside disks of gas and dust that circle young stars, where rocky pieces crash and stick together to build bigger bodies.
After most of the gas is gone, the leftover dust and rubble form what astronomers call a debris disk.
Studying these disks helps scientists understand how rocky planets like Earth, and our Moon, came to be.
